title: Identity & Access Management
oneLiner: Control who can do what: IAM users, roles, policies, temporary credentials, and multi-account guardrails.
examWeightNote: Part of Design Secure Architectures — the largest exam domain at 30%.
objectives: Differentiate IAM users, groups, roles, and policies, and know when to use a role over long-lived keys.
Explain how EC2 instance profiles and STS provide temporary credentials.
Use AWS Organizations and Service Control Policies (SCPs) to set account-wide guardrails.
Apply least-privilege and evaluate how policies combine (explicit deny wins).

services.name: AWS IAM
services.purpose: Users, groups, roles, and identity-/resource-based policies that authorize API actions.

services.name: AWS STS
services.purpose: Issues short-lived, automatically rotated temporary credentials when a role is assumed.

services.name: IAM Roles / Instance Profiles
services.purpose: Let EC2, Lambda, and cross-account principals get permissions without stored keys.

services.name: AWS Organizations & SCPs
services.purpose: Central multi-account management with guardrails that cap the maximum permissions in member accounts.

services.name: IAM Identity Center
services.purpose: Central workforce SSO and permission sets across many accounts.

keyConcepts: Prefer IAM roles (temporary credentials via STS) over long-lived access keys — especially for EC2, Lambda, and cross-account access.
Policy evaluation: an explicit Deny always overrides any Allow; without an explicit allow, access is implicitly denied.
An SCP sets the maximum permissions an account can have — it never grants access on its own; you still need IAM policies inside the account.
Grant least privilege: start minimal and add permissions; use conditions (e.g. source IP, MFA) to tighten access.
Never embed access keys in code or AMIs — attach an instance profile/role instead.

scenarios.scenario: An application on EC2 needs to read objects from an S3 bucket. A developer hard-coded IAM access keys into the app config to make it work.
scenarios.question: What is the recommended, most secure way to give the EC2 app access to S3?

options.label: Store the access keys in an environment variable instead
Attach an IAM role (instance profile) granting S3 read access to the EC2 instance
Make the S3 bucket public and remove the keys
Create a new IAM user for the app and rotate keys weekly

scenarios.explanation: An instance profile lets EC2 obtain temporary, auto-rotated credentials via STS — no long-lived keys to leak. Hard-coding or env-var keys and making buckets public are all insecure.

scenarios.scenario: Your company has 40 AWS accounts under Organizations. Security wants to guarantee no one in any member account can disable CloudTrail, regardless of their IAM permissions.
scenarios.question: Which control enforces this account-wide guardrail?

options.label: A Service Control Policy (SCP) that denies cloudtrail:StopLogging
An IAM policy attached to every user in every account
Enabling MFA on the root user

scenarios.explanation: SCPs set the maximum permissions for member accounts. A deny SCP on cloudtrail:StopLogging blocks the action even for admins. Attaching IAM policies to every user is error-prone and not centrally enforced.

quiz.question: Which credential type does STS issue when a role is assumed?
options: Permanent access keys
Temporary, automatically-expiring credentials
A username and password
An SSH key pair
quiz.explanation: AWS STS vends short-lived credentials that expire automatically, which is why roles are preferred over long-lived access keys.

quiz.question: In IAM policy evaluation, what happens when one policy allows an action and another explicitly denies it?
options: The Allow wins
The Deny wins
It depends on which was created first
The action requires MFA
quiz.explanation: An explicit Deny always overrides any Allow. This is a core rule of IAM policy evaluation.

quiz.question: What does an AWS Organizations Service Control Policy (SCP) do?
options: Grants permissions to users directly
Sets the maximum permissions available in member accounts
Encrypts data at rest
Creates temporary credentials
quiz.answer: Sets the maximum permissions available in member accounts
quiz.explanation: SCPs are guardrails — they cap what identities in an account can do but never grant permissions themselves; IAM policies still grant the actual access.

quiz.question: What is the best practice for giving a Lambda function access to a DynamoDB table?
options: Embed access keys in the function code
Assign the function an execution role with a least-privilege policy
Make the table publicly accessible
Use the account root credentials
quiz.answer: Assign the function an execution role with a least-privilege policy
quiz.explanation: Lambda uses an execution role for temporary credentials. Grant only the specific DynamoDB actions/resource it needs (least privilege).

quiz.question: What is the key difference between an IAM user and an IAM role?
options: A user has permanent credentials for a person/app; a role is assumed to get temporary credentials
A role can only be used by AWS support
A user cannot have any policies attached
There is no difference
quiz.answer: A user has permanent credentials for a person/app; a role is assumed to get temporary credentials
quiz.explanation: IAM users represent a person or application with long-lived credentials, while roles are assumed by trusted principals (services, users, other accounts) to receive temporary credentials — the preferred approach.

quiz.question: Which is a recommended best practice for the AWS account root user?
options: Use it for all daily administration
Share its credentials with the team
Enable MFA and avoid using it for everyday tasks
Create access keys for automation with it
quiz.answer: Enable MFA and avoid using it for everyday tasks
quiz.explanation: The root user should have MFA enabled and be locked away — day-to-day work should use IAM users/roles with least privilege, not root.

quiz.question: How should you grant an application in Account A access to an S3 bucket in Account B?
options: Share long-lived access keys from Account B
Make the bucket public
Create a role in Account B that Account A can assume (cross-account role)
Merge the two accounts
quiz.answer: Create a role in Account B that Account A can assume (cross-account role)
quiz.explanation: Cross-account access is done by defining a role in the resource account with a trust policy allowing the other account to assume it — no shared long-lived keys required.

quiz.question: What does the principle of least privilege recommend?
options: Grant admin access to everyone for convenience
Grant only the permissions required to perform a task, and no more
Deny all access at all times
Use the root user for scoped tasks
quiz.answer: Grant only the permissions required to perform a task, and no more
quiz.explanation: Least privilege means starting with minimal permissions and adding only what's needed, reducing blast radius if credentials are compromised.

quiz.question: What is AWS IAM Identity Center primarily used for?
options: Encrypting data at rest
Centralized workforce single sign-on and permission sets across multiple accounts
Distributing content globally
Running serverless functions
quiz.answer: Centralized workforce single sign-on and permission sets across multiple accounts
quiz.explanation: IAM Identity Center (successor to AWS SSO) provides central SSO and assigns permission sets to users/groups across many accounts in an organization.
